title: Where the data comes from
claim: The tracker counts payloads listed in CelesTrak's public satellite catalogue (SATCAT) that have not yet decayed.
method: Read from parse_satcat in server.py: only object type PAYLOAD, no decay date, Earth orbit.
limitations: Rocket bodies and debris are not counted. Objects missing from public catalogues (some military or very small objects) are not counted either.

title: How active, inactive and unknown are decided
claim: Status codes + P B S X count as active, the code - counts as inactive, and every other code counts as unknown.
method: Rule in server.py (ACTIVE_CODES and classify). Compare it with CelesTrak's published list of status codes before presenting.
limitations: Status is reported by the catalogue and can lag reality. A satellite can fail days before its code changes.

title: Counts are internally consistent
claim: Active, inactive and unknown add up to the total, and the total equals the number of rows shown in the table.
method: Checked by build_research.py every time the data is rebuilt.
limitations: Proves the arithmetic only, not that the catalogue is complete.

title: No duplicate satellites
claim: Each NORAD catalogue ID appears once in the data.
method: Checked by build_research.py every time the data is rebuilt.
limitations: Two records could still describe the same hardware under different IDs.

title: Orbit figures agree with physics
claim: For each satellite, the reported period matches the period Kepler's third law gives from its perigee and apogee.
method: Semi-major axis a = (perigee + apogee) / 2 + 6378.137 km, then T = 2π√(a³/μ). Tolerance 0.5%.
limitations: Assumes catalogue perigee and apogee are altitudes above Earth's surface (confirm in CelesTrak's format notes). Two-body physics only, so it checks consistency, not real accuracy.

title: Why inactive satellites matter
claim: An inactive satellite cannot manoeuvre to avoid a collision, so it adds to debris risk until it decays or is moved out of the way.
method: Standard point in orbital debris literature. The 2009 Iridium 33 and Cosmos 2251 collision involved a defunct satellite.
limitations: Inactive does not always mean uncontrolled. Some are passivated or parked in disposal orbits.
